title: Ἀνδροφόνος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 45 (= Perry 32). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἄνθρωπόν τις ἀποκτείνας ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκείνου συγγενῶν ἐδιώκετο· γενόμενος δὲ κατὰ τὸν Νεῖλον ποταμόν, λύκου αὐτῷ ἀπαντήσαντος, φοβηθεὶς ἀνέβη ἐπὶ δένδρου τῷ ποταμῷ παρακειμένου καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐκρύπτετο.
sentences.tr: Anthrōpon tis apokteinas hypo tōn ekeinou syngenōn ediōketo· genomenos de kata ton Neilon potamon, lykou autōi apantēsantos, phobētheis anebē epi dendrou tōi potamōi parakeimenou kai ekei ekrypteto.
sentences.l: Someone, having-killed a man, was being pursued by that man's kinsmen; and having-come-to-be by the river Nile, a wolf having-met him, having-become-afraid he went up onto a tree lying beside the river, and there he was hiding.
sentences.i: A man who had killed someone was being hunted by the dead man's kin; when he came to the river Nile a wolf met him, and in his fear he climbed a tree standing by the river and hid there.
sentences.n: The fable's engine, plainly on show: two aorist participles (ἀποκτείνας, φοβηθείς) and a genitive absolute (λύκου … ἀπαντήσαντος) carry every circumstance, leaving one main verb to each clause. κατὰ τὸν Νεῖλον ποταμόν, κατά with the accusative, is 'down at, over against' the Nile. The Egyptian setting is what brings the crocodile.

sentences.t: Θεασάμενος δὲ ἐνταῦθα δράκοντα κατ’ αὐτοῦ διαιρόμενον, ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸν ποταμὸν καθῆκεν· ἐν δὲ τῷ ποταμῷ κροκόδειλος αὐτὸν κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Theasamenos de entautha drakonta kat' autou diairomenon, heauton eis ton potamon kathēken· en de tōi potamōi krokodeilos auton katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And having-caught-sight-of there a serpent rearing-itself-up against him, he let himself down into the river; and in the river a crocodile made a feast of him.
sentences.i: But seeing a snake there rearing up at him, he dropped himself into the river — and in the river a crocodile made a meal of him.
sentences.n: δράκων is any large snake, not the fabulous dragon. κατεθοινήσατο is κατά + θοινάομαι, 'feast on': stronger than 'ate'. The three places he passes through — the ground, the tree, the river — are laid out so that the moral can name them as earth, air and water.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοῖς ἐναγέσι τῶν ἀνθρώπων οὔτε γῆς, οὔτε ἀέρος, οὔτε ὕδατος στοιχεῖον ἀσφαλές ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti tois enagesi tōn anthrōpōn oute gēs, oute aeros, oute hydatos stoicheion asphales esti.
sentences.l: The story shows that for the accursed among men neither the element of earth, nor of air, nor of water is safe.
sentences.n: ἐναγής is a religious word: a man polluted by blood-guilt, under a curse and shunned by gods and men. στοιχεῖον is 'element' in the old physical sense; the three named answer the three creatures of the tale.
